# Paris Style: A Guide to What's Trending in the City of Light

**PARIS, France (CNN)** -- In a city renowned as the birthplace of the avant-garde, keeping pace with the latest trends can prove challenging. Here is a concise guide to what's currently capturing the attention of Parisians.

## Tecktonik: The Latest Dance Craze

Parisian youth have always embraced emerging trends with enthusiasm, and their latest obsession is Tecktonik—a fusion dance style typically accompanied by spiked hair and neon accessories. Keep an eye out for groups of young dancers congregating outside the Trocadéro, where, if fortune favors you, you might even witness an impromptu Tecktonik-versus-breakdance showdown.

## Le Scrapbooking

For Paris's more contemplative residents, scrapbooking has emerged as the craze of choice. Visit Le Temple Du Scrap (13 Rue Ernest Cresson) to discover an array of decorative papers, trimmings, ribbons, and other embellishments perfect for the pursuit.

## Cycling Through the City

While much of Paris lends itself beautifully to walking, the city's affordable bike-share program, Vélib—launched in 2007—offers an even more convenient way to explore. Thousands of bicycles are stationed throughout the city, with docking points positioned roughly 300 meters apart. The first thirty minutes of each ride are complimentary, though a credit card is required for registration. Once equipped with your bike, you'll be ready to navigate the cobblestone streets of Montmartre or glide along the banks of the Seine.

## Café Culture Hotspots

The quintessential image of the smoke-filled Parisian café has largely relocated to the sidewalks, following a smoking ban in bars and restaurants enacted at the end of 2007. Quel dommage! During the winter months, the most coveted café spots are those featuring heated terraces, where patrons can still enjoy a cigarette alongside their petit café crème—provided they remain outdoors. A turtleneck and beret are recommended, offering both warmth and Parisian flair.

## Massages at the Mosque

Home to a substantial Muslim population, Paris boasts La Grande Mosquée de Paris (rue Geoffroy St. Hilaire) as a testament to this rich cultural presence. The building's exterior is truly stunning, while its interior proves even more breathtaking. Indulge in a massage at the hammam, or Turkish bath, for an experience so immersive you might momentarily believe yourself transported to Morocco. Afterward, unwind with a cup of mint tea in the courtyard. Note that visiting hours are designated separately for men and women, so it's advisable to confirm the schedule in advance.

## Subway Style

Navigating the Paris Métro can, admittedly, be an ordeal—between striking transit workers and less-than-pristine platforms, the experience often falls short of glamorous. Yet amid this occasionally dreary underground network lies a genuine gem: the Palais Royal entrance to the Palais Royal–Musée du Louvre station. As with so much in Paris, this stop transcends mere function to become a work of art in its own right, courtesy of French artist Jean-Michel Othoniel. His installation of vividly colored glass beads is nothing short of enchanting, and the nearby Place Colette offers an ideal vantage point for people-watching—simply find a seat and take in the scene.

# The New Paris: Trends and Traditions in the City of Light

Paris, ever the city of reinvention, continues to surprise both residents and visitors with an intriguing mix of contemporary trends and evolving cultural practices. Beyond the postcard images of the Eiffel Tower and Louvre, a different, more dynamic Paris is emerging—one shaped by youth culture, practical innovation, and shifting social habits.

## Tecktonik: The Dance Craze Taking Over Parisian Streets

A striking new subculture has taken hold among the city's youth: Tecktonik. This high-energy fusion dance style, characterized by rapid arm movements, gravity-defying spiked hairstyles, and vibrant neon accessories, has become something of a visual and cultural phenomenon. Groups of enthusiastic dancers can frequently be spotted practicing their moves near the Trocadero, drawn perhaps by its open plazas and stunning views of the Eiffel Tower. What began as an underground movement has blossomed into a full-fledged youth culture, complete with its own fashion sensibilities and community identity, offering a glimpse into the more experimental side of Parisian street life.

## Scrapbooking: A Quieter Pursuit Gains Popularity

In contrast to the flashy energy of Tecktonik, another hobby has been quietly winning over Paris's more contemplative residents: scrapbooking. This meditative, creative pastime has found a devoted following among those seeking a relaxing way to preserve memories and express artistic sensibilities. Le Temple Du Scrap has emerged as a go-to destination for enthusiasts, stocking an impressive array of supplies including decorative paper, trimmings, ribbons, and other embellishments needed to create beautifully crafted keepsakes. The rise of scrapbooking speaks to a different facet of Parisian life—one characterized by patience, nostalgia, and hands-on creativity.

## Vélib: Revolutionizing Urban Transportation

For visitors and locals alike wanting to explore Paris efficiently and affordably, the Vélib bike-sharing scheme has proven to be a genuine game-changer since its launch in 2007. This innovative program has strategically placed thousands of bicycles at docking stations positioned roughly every 300 meters throughout the city, making it remarkably convenient to pick up a bike in one location and drop it off near your destination. The system has not only reduced traffic congestion and pollution but has also given visitors a new, active way to experience the city—pedaling past historic monuments, along the Seine, or through charming neighborhoods at their own pace, all while enjoying an affordable alternative to taxis or public transit.

## The Smoking Ban and the Evolution of Café Culture

When France implemented a nationwide smoking ban in bars and restaurants in late 2007, many wondered how it would affect the iconic Parisian café culture, so deeply intertwined with the ritual of smoking alongside coffee and conversation. The answer emerged in the form of adaptation rather than abandonment: outdoor terraces, once a seasonal pleasure, have been transformed into year-round social hubs through the addition of heating lamps and enclosed but open-air spaces. This ingenious solution has allowed patrons to continue enjoying their cigarettes alongside their espressos and café crèmes, preserving a beloved tradition while complying with public health regulations. The result is a café scene that feels both familiar and renewed, with terraces bustling with activity regardless of the season.

## La Grande Mosquée de Paris: Architecture and Relaxation Combined

For those seeking a cultural experience paired with genuine relaxation, La Grande Mosquée de Paris offers a truly memorable destination. Beyond its breathtaking architecture—featuring intricate tilework, elegant courtyards, and a striking minaret that reflects North African and Moorish influences—the mosque complex is also home to an authentic hammam offering traditional massages and steam bath treatments. Visitors can wander through the serene gardens and admire the craftsmanship of the building before indulging in a rejuvenating hammam experience, making it a rare opportunity to combine sightseeing with wellness in a single, culturally rich setting.

---

Together, these five facets of contemporary Paris—from neon-lit dance crazes to tranquil scrapbooking sessions, from eco-friendly bike shares to adapted café culture and cultural wellness retreats—illustrate a city that honors its traditions while continuously evolving to meet the changing tastes and needs of its residents and visitors.

# Parisian Trends: Where Tradition Meets Innovation

Paris, a city eternally celebrated for its historic boulevards, iconic monuments, and timeless elegance, is also a vibrant hub of contemporary culture and evolving urban lifestyles. Beneath the surface of its classical architecture and centuries-old traditions, a dynamic mix of modern trends is reshaping how both locals and visitors experience the French capital. From dance floors to bike lanes, and from steam rooms to sidewalk cafés, Paris in the twenty-first century offers a fascinating blend of the old and the new.

## The Tecktonik Phenomenon

One of the most striking youth movements to emerge from Paris in recent years is Tecktonik, an energetic dance style characterized by rapid arm movements, jumps, and an electro-pop soundtrack. Born in the suburbs and popularized through nightclubs and viral internet videos, Tecktonik quickly became a cultural phenomenon among French teenagers and young adults. Dancers, often sporting distinctive fashion—skinny jeans, asymmetrical haircuts, and neon accessories—gather in clubs and public spaces to showcase their moves. This trend illustrates how Paris continues to serve as a breeding ground for youth culture that spreads far beyond its borders, fueled by social media and a generation eager to express identity through movement and style.

## The Nostalgic Charm of Scrapbooking

In contrast to the high-energy world of Tecktonik, scrapbooking has emerged as a quieter yet equally significant trend among Parisians seeking a creative and nostalgic outlet. This hobby, which involves compiling photographs, memorabilia, and decorative elements into personalized albums, has found a devoted following in the city. Specialty boutiques and workshops have sprung up, offering enthusiasts the tools and inspiration to preserve memories in artistic ways. Scrapbooking's rise in popularity speaks to a broader desire among urban dwellers to slow down, reflect, and engage in tactile, meaningful activities that stand in contrast to the fast-paced digital world.

## Velib: Revolutionizing Urban Transport

Perhaps no innovation has transformed daily life in Paris more visibly than the Velib bike-sharing scheme. Launched to address urban congestion and promote eco-friendly transportation, Velib allows residents and tourists alike to rent bicycles from stations scattered throughout the city and return them at any other location. This system has not only reduced reliance on cars but has also encouraged a healthier, more active lifestyle among city dwellers. Cyclists now weave through historic streets and past famous landmarks, merging the practicality of modern transport with the timeless beauty of the Parisian cityscape. Velib stands as a testament to how urban planning can successfully marry sustainability with convenience.

## Café Culture in a Smoke-Free Era

The traditional Parisian café, long associated with plumes of cigarette smoke and animated conversation, has undergone a notable transformation following the implementation of France's smoking ban. This legislative change has altered the atmosphere of cafés across the city, prompting many establishments to adapt their outdoor seating areas to accommodate smokers while creating fresher, more inclusive environments indoors. The shift has sparked debate about the loss of a certain bohemian ambiance once tied to smoky interiors, yet it has also opened doors to a broader clientele, including families and health-conscious patrons. Café culture, ever resilient, continues to serve as a cornerstone of Parisian social life, adapting to new regulations while preserving its role as a space for connection and leisure.

## Relaxation at the Grande Mosquée

Amid the bustling trends of dance, hobbies, and transportation, the Grande Mosquée de Paris offers a serene escape through its traditional hammam and spa treatments. This historic mosque, with its stunning Moorish architecture, houses a authentic bathhouse where visitors can indulge in exfoliating scrubs, steam baths, and massages rooted in North African traditions. The experience provides a stark contrast to the fast-paced trends elsewhere in the city, inviting patrons to slow down and immerse themselves in a centuries-old ritual of relaxation and rejuvenation. The Grande Mosquée's spa exemplifies how Paris honors its multicultural heritage while offering modern city dwellers a much-needed retreat from urban stress.

## Conclusion: A City of Contrasts and Continuities

Together, these diverse trends—from the electrifying moves of Tecktonik to the meditative art of scrapbooking, from the practical ingenuity of Velib to the evolving rituals of café culture, and finally to the timeless tranquility found at the Grande Mosquée—reveal a Paris that is constantly reinventing itself while remaining deeply connected to its roots. This blend of historic character and modern innovation creates a rich tapestry of experiences that cater to a wide range of interests and lifestyles. Whether one seeks youthful energy on the dance floor, practical solutions for urban mobility, or a peaceful retreat steeped in tradition, Paris offers something for everyone. It is this very duality—the ability to honor the past while embracing the future—that makes the city an endlessly fascinating destination for both visitors and those fortunate enough to call it home.

Paris, the capital city of France, stands as one of the world's most iconic and beloved destinations. Known as the "City of Light," Paris has captivated travelers, artists, and dreamers for centuries with its timeless architecture, rich history, and vibrant culture.

Home to world-renowned landmarks such as the Eiffel Tower, the Louvre Museum, and Notre-Dame Cathedral, Paris attracts millions of visitors each year. The city's charming streets, sidewalk cafés, and stunning gardens along the Seine River create an atmosphere that blends old-world elegance with modern sophistication.

Paris frequently makes international headlines, and news organizations like CNN regularly cover stories emanating from the city—ranging from political developments at the Élysée Palace to cultural events, fashion shows, and major international summits. Beyond its iconic sites, Paris is celebrated for its culinary excellence, with countless bistros, patisseries, and Michelin-starred restaurants offering exquisite French cuisine. The city's museums, including the Musée d'Orsay and Centre Pompidou, showcase incredible artistic achievements spanning centuries.

Whether covered in international news broadcasts or experienced firsthand by tourists, Paris continues to symbolize romance, culture, and sophistication. Its enduring appeal ensures that France's capital remains a focal point of global attention, whether through major news coverage by outlets like CNN or through the millions of personal stories created by visitors who fall in love with this magnificent city every year.

# Paris Like a Local: The Neighborhoods and Trends Redefining the City of Light

**PARIS** — Forget the exhausting sprint between the Eiffel Tower and the Louvre. A new generation of travelers is discovering that the real Paris—the one Parisians actually love—exists in the spaces between the monuments, in neighborhood wine bars, converted industrial spaces, and markets where the city's future is being written in real time.

Here's where savvy visitors are heading this year.

## The Rise of the "Coin de Quartier"

Parisians have always been fiercely loyal to their neighborhood, or *quartier*, and that hyperlocal culture is now the city's biggest draw. Areas once overlooked by guidebooks—the 11th arrondissement's Rue de la Roquette, the increasingly bohemian Belleville, and the quietly gentrifying Batignolles in the 17th—are where visitors are finding the Paris of Instagram fantasy without the crowds.

"Tourists used to ask us how to get to the Marais," says Camille Durand, who runs walking tours focused on residential neighborhoods. "Now they ask where Parisians actually eat lunch on a Tuesday."

## Natural Wine Is Having a Moment (Still)

The natural wine bar boom that started nearly a decade ago hasn't slowed—it's matured. Spots like **Le Verre Volé** near Canal Saint-Martin remain essential, but newer arrivals in the 10th and 20th arrondissements are pairing biodynamic bottles with hyper-seasonal small plates, creating a distinctly Parisian answer to the small-bar dining trend sweeping global cities. Expect handwritten chalkboard menus, no reservations, and standing room only by 7:30 p.m.

## Canal Saint-Martin's Quiet Comeback

Once the epicenter of hipster Paris, Canal Saint-Martin faded slightly from the spotlight—and that's precisely its appeal now. Sunday afternoons still bring locals with wine bottles and baguettes to the canal's edge, but the surrounding streets have quietly filled with independent bookshops, ceramics studios, and coffee roasters like **Boot Café**, tucked into a former shoe repair shop.

## The Covered Passages Renaissance

Paris's 19th-century covered shopping arcades—*passages couverts*—are experiencing an unexpected revival. **Passage du Grand Cerf** and **Galerie Vivienne** have become destinations for independent designers, vintage booksellers, and specialty shops that feel worlds away from the polished boutiques of the Champs-Élysées. They offer what travelers increasingly want: shelter from both weather and crowds, plus a genuine sense of discovery.

## Markets Over Museums

While the Louvre remains a bucket-list essential, food-forward travelers are prioritizing market visits as cultural experiences in their own right. **Marché des Enfants Rouges**, Paris's oldest covered market, draws visitors for lunch among Parisians shopping for dinner. Saturday mornings at **Marché Bastille** offer a similarly immersive slice of daily life, stretching for nearly a mile with cheese vendors who've held the same stall for decades.

## Where to Stay: Small and Storied

The boutique hotel trend continues shifting away from grand palace hotels toward smaller, design-conscious properties in residential neighborhoods. Travelers are seeking out converted townhouses and apartment-style stays in the 9th and 11th arrondissements, prioritizing proximity to daily life over proximity to landmarks.

## The Bottom Line

The through-line connecting all these trends: an appetite for texture over spectacle. Today's Paris visitor wants to sip coffee where the barista knows regulars by name, not just photograph the Eiffel Tower from a predictable angle.

The monuments aren't going anywhere. But increasingly, the itinerary that matters is the one built around the city's actual rhythm—unhurried, deeply local, and refreshingly imperfect.

*Bonne visite.*

# Paris Right Now: The City of Light's Latest Obsessions

**PARIS** — Forget everything you think you know about the Paris of black berets and mime artists. Today's City of Light is pulsating with a different kind of energy — one measured in bike bell rings, oat milk foam, and TikTok choreography performed along the Seine.

## The Dance Floor Has Moved Outside

On any given evening from May through September, Parisians are ditching stuffy clubs for impromptu dance sessions along the Canal Saint-Martin and the quays near Pont des Arts. "Guinguette" culture — those old-school outdoor dance parties once associated with your grandparents' generation — has been resurrected by twenty- and thirty-somethings who've discovered that swing dancing to a Bluetooth speaker beats a €15 cocktail any day.

Meanwhile, TikTok has birthed its own hyperlocal phenomenon: choreographed flash mobs outside the Louvre pyramid, performed with the kind of ironic detachment only the French can pull off. Nobody's quite sure if it's satire or sincere. That, apparently, is the point.

## Two Wheels, Zero Chill

Paris has fully committed to its bike-topia era. Since the pandemic-era cycling lanes went from "temporary" to permanent fixtures, the city has seen a two-wheeled renaissance that borders on religious devotion. Vélib' bike-share stations now outnumber certain boulangeries (a genuinely controversial statistic among locals).

The real status symbol, though? A vintage bike — the older and more rust-speckled, the better — paired with a wicker basket holding nothing more than a baguette and a single, perfectly posed bouquet of flowers. It's giving "effortless," but make no mistake: hours of Pinterest research went into that aesthetic.

## Coffee Culture Gets a Glow-Up

The traditional Parisian café — where a single espresso bought you two hours of people-watching rights — hasn't disappeared, but it's sharing the spotlight with a new wave of specialty coffee shops obsessed with single-origin beans and oat milk lattes served in ceramic cups that look suspiciously Instagram-optimized.

Neighborhoods like the Marais and Belleville are now dotted with these hybrid spaces — part café, part co-working hub, part art gallery — where twenty-somethings nurse €6 flat whites for the better part of a workday. Traditionalists grumble. The lines out the door suggest nobody's listening.

## The Metro's Secret Celebrity Stops

Even the Paris Métro — that gloriously unglamorous underground workhorse — has developed cult favorites among in-the-know riders and tourists alike.

**Arts et Métiers** (Line 11) feels like stepping into a Jules Verne fever dream, with copper-paneled walls resembling a steampunk submarine. **Concorde** (Line 12) turns your commute into a spelling lesson, its walls tiled with letters spelling out the Declaration of the Rights of Man. And **Louvre-Rivoli** (Line 1) offers actual museum replicas on the platform — because why wait in line upstairs when you can admire a sphinx while waiting for your train?

Savvy locals now treat "stop-hopping" — riding a few extra stations just to snap a stylish alcove — as a legitimate weekend activity.

## The Bottom Line

Paris remains gloriously, stubbornly Parisian — cigarette breaks, existential shrugs, and all — but the city's latest cultural currents prove it's not stuck in amber. Whether you're canal-side swing dancing, oat-latte sipping, or metro-hopping for the 'gram, the French capital is having a moment. Multiple moments, actually. All at once, with a coffee in hand.

*Just don't call it a trend to a Parisian's face. They'll insist they invented it decades ago — and somehow, they might be right.*

Forget the three-hour Louvre queue. Paris in 2024-2025 is having a moment defined by underground wine bars, immersive art you can wander through blindfolded (almost), and a renewed love affair with its own waterways. Here's what's actually drawing crowds right now.

Everyone's done the daytime Catacombs shuffle. Now, limited nighttime tours let visitors explore the ossuary by lantern-light, with far fewer tourists and considerably more atmosphere. Book months ahead—these sell out fast, and for good reason.

**Marché aux Puces de Saint-Ouen** remains the classic, but savvy visitors are heading to smaller weekend brocantes in the Marais and Batignolles for vintage Le Creuset, mid-century ephemera, and haggling practice with actual Parisians.

# Paris, 2008: The City of Light Gets a Modern Makeover

*Notes from a season of watching the French capital reinvent itself*

There's a peculiar energy in Paris this year—the ancient bones of the city dressed up in surprisingly playful new clothes. As someone who's spent the better part of a decade watching trends ripple through this city's arrondissements, 2008 feels different. Paris isn't just preserving its past; it's remixing it.

## The Vélib' Revolution

You can't walk two blocks without seeing them now: those sturdy grey bicycles, docked in rows at silver stations that have sprouted across the city like mechanical mushrooms. Vélib'—launched last summer—has utterly transformed how Parisians move through their own city. For roughly €1 a day, anyone can grab a bike and pedal past the Louvre instead of queuing for the Métro.

I watched a businessman in a suit jacket wobble slightly as he mounted one outside the Bastille station, phone still pressed to his ear. Locals grumbled at first—more competition for sidewalk space, more tourists blocking bike lanes—but even skeptics are converting. There's something wonderfully democratic about it: the same bike that carries a banker to La Défense might carry a student to the Sorbonne an hour later.

## Scrapbooking, Sacré Bleu

American friends visiting this year keep asking about "le scrapbooking"—and yes, it's arrived, filtering in through expat communities and design boutiques in the Marais. French crafting shops now stock washi tape and acid-free paper alongside their usual art supplies. It's a curious cultural exchange: the French, who've always approached photography and memory-keeping with a certain minimalist chic, are now experimenting with the maximalist, glitter-glue enthusiasm of American scrapbook culture. Whether it sticks past this season remains to be seen.

## Dancing in the Streets (Literally)

Wednesday and Friday evenings, head to the Seine's edges near Pont de Sully and you'll find impromptu salsa gatherings—no permits, no fuss, just speakers and hip movement. The "Guédra" and various Afrobeat-influenced dance styles are having a moment in clubs from Belleville to Pigalle, brought in by the city's vibrant West African diaspora. Meanwhile, retro dance nights—swing, Lindy Hop—pack out small venues in the 11th arrondissement, young Parisians in vintage dress twirling like it's 1938.

## Café Culture, Reconsidered

The traditional zinc-countered café isn't going anywhere, thank god, but there's a new crop of hybrid spaces emerging—part café, part gallery, part reading room. Wifi (still called "le wifi" with a shrug of resignation by purists) is becoming less of a novelty and more of an expectation, even as the old guard insists real conversation happens without a laptop screen glowing between friends.

## Offbeat Paris

For travelers tired of the standard Eiffel Tower photo-op, whispers point to the Catacombs' lesser-known tunnels, the hidden petite ceinture (the abandoned circular railway now colonized by urban explorers and wildflowers), and Musée des Egouts de Paris—yes, the sewer museum—for those who want their Paris a little more pungent and peculiar.

---

*The City of Light, it turns out, still knows how to surprise.*
